One possible explanation put forth by Keenan and Comrie (1977) to account for this pattern is that subject relative clauses are easier to process in online comprehension. Since then, a large body of experimental work has emerged investigating the relative difficulty of processing subject and object relative clauses. Using a wide variety of psycholinguistic measures, a subject processing advantage in relative clauses has been clearly observed for English (self-paced reading time: King & Just, 1991; ERP: King & Kutas, 1995; PET: Stromswold et al., 1996, Caplan et al., 1998, Caplan et al., 1999, Caplan et al., 2000; fMRI: Just et al., 1996, Caplan et al., 2002, Cooke et al., 2002, Constable et al., 2004, Chen et al., 2006, Caplan et al., 2008; eye-tracking: Traxler et al., 2002), as well as for other languages including Dutch (Frazier 1987), German (Mecklinger et al., 1995, Schriefers et al., 1995, Münte et al., 1997, Bader and Meng, 1999, Schwartz, 2007), French (Frauenfelder et al., 1980, Holmes and O’Regan, 1981, Cohen and Mehler, 1996), Hebrew (Friedmann and Novogrodsky, 2004, Arnon, 2005), Turkish (Kahraman et al., 2010), and Russian (Polinsky, 2011, Levy et al., 2013). Theories of relative clause processing that have been put forth to explain these results have tended to focus either on the linear/temporal distance between the filler (in this case, the head noun) and the gap (inside the relative clause), or, alternatively, on the grammatical function of the relativized noun, whereby relativization on subjects is inherently easier to process. One obvious way to distinguish between these sets of theories is to look at languages that have prenominal relative clauses. In these languages, distance between the gap and filler will be shorter in object relative clauses, so if the subject processing advantage seen in languages with postnominal relative clauses, like English, is due to linear/temporal distance between the filler and gap, then we would expect object relative clauses to be easier. If, on the other hand, relativization on subjects is universally easier to process, then such languages should show the familiar preference for subject relative clauses. The subject gap processing advantage has been consistently replicated in two languages with prenominal relative clauses: Japanese (self-paced reading time: Kanno and Nakamura, 2001, Miyamoto and Nakamura, 2003, Ishizuka et al., 2003; ERP: Ueno & Garnsey, 2008) and Korean (self-paced reading time: Kwon et al., 2006, Kwon, 2008; eye-tracking: Kwon et al., 2010; ERP: Kwon et al., 2013), seeming to argue against a simple filler-gap distance account. For Chinese, however, mixed results have been reported: Hsiao and Gibson’s initial (2003) report that Mandarin showed a preference for object relative clauses, supporting the linear distance account, has been followed up by a rich set of experimental studies, some of which replicate the object-relative clause preference (self-paced reading time: Lin and Garnsey, 2007, Chen et al., 2008, Lin, 2010, Gibson and Wu, 2013; maze-task: Qiao et al., 2012), some of which rather indicate a preference for subject relative clauses (self-paced reading time: Lin & Bever, 2006, Chen et al., 2010; Vasishth et al., 2013, Xu et al., 2019), and some of which argue that both SRCs and ORCs show distinct processing costs in different ERP measures (Bulut et al., 2018). For Cantonese, an object relative clause preference has been reported for child language, at least based on production (Yip & Matthews, 2007). Although debate continues over how best to understand the variability observed across the Mandarin and Cantonese data, on the whole what seems clear from work on the processing of prenominal relative clauses is that (a) facilitated processing for subject gaps cannot be wholly attributed to the linear distance between the gap position and the filler (given the residual subject relative clause preference observed in the Japanese and Korean studies) and (b) other factors must also impact the ease of relative clause processing, given the differences in the processing profile for Mandarin/Cantonese (at the least, in the greater variability observed across studies). Submit a story 1 Subject Preference and Ergativity Maria Polinskya, Carlos Gomez Galloa , Peter Graffb, Ekaterina Kravtchenkoc Harvard Universitya, MITb, University of California Santa Cruzc Abstract This paper presents the first-ever processing experiment on relativization in Avar, an ergative language with prenominal relatives. The results show no processing difference between the ergative subject gap and the absolutive object gap. The absolutive subject gap, however, is processed much faster. We propose a principled explanation for this result. On the one hand, Avar has a subject preference (cf. the Accessibility Hierarchy, Keenan and Comrie, 1977), which would make the processing of the ergative and the absolutive subject gap easier than the processing of the absolutive object gap. On the other hand, the ergative DP in a relative clause serves as a strong cue that allows the parser to project the remainder of the clause, including the absolutive object DP (cf. Marantz, 1991, 2000); such morphological cueing favors the absolutive object gap. Thus, two processing preferences, the one for subject relatives and the other for morphologically cued clauses, cancel each other out in terms of processing difficulty. As a result, reading time results for the ergative subject and absolutive object relative clauses are very similar. The overall processing results are significantly different from what is found in accusative languages, where subject preference and morphological cueing reinforce each other, leading to a strong transitive subject advantage. Keywords: ergativity, A-bar movement, relativization, Avar, processing 2 1. Introduction Every natural language is capable of forming relative clauses, and their patterning across languages displays one of the most robust generalizations attested in cross-linguistic research. This generalization has been captured in the Accessibility Hierarchy (AH) of Keenan and Comrie (1977, 1979). According to the AH, there is an ordering of grammatical relations such that, within a given language, if one grammatical position can relativize with a gap, then all grammatical positions to the left of this position on the hierarchy must also be able to relativize with a gap: (1) subject > direct object > indirect object > oblique object > possessor > object of comparison That is, if a language can relativize obliques, it can also relativize direct and indirect objects and subjects. If a language can relativize objects, it can also relativize subjects, but not necessarily obliques. A critical claim behind the AH is that every language should be able to relativize its highest argument even if nothing else on the scale in (1) is accessible to relativization. The AH was intended as a cross-linguistic generalization on the distribution of different types of relative clauses in various languages: from English, whose relativization is omnivorous, to many Austronesian languages, which only allow the relativization of subjects/external arguments (cf. Keenan, 1976; Gartner et al., 2006; Chung and Polinsky, 2009). More recently, the AH has also been evoked in the explanation of the subject preference in the processing of relative clauses in English. Subject preference has been noted in first and second language acquisition (see O'Grady, 2010 for an overview), and in other languages: German (Schwartz, 2007, a.o.), Dutch (Frazier, 1987), Russian (e.g., 3 Polinsky, 2011), Hebrew (e.g., Friedmann and Novogrodsky, 2004), Japanese (Miyamoto and Nakamura, 2003; Ueno and Garnsey, 2008), and Korean (Kwon et al., 2010), to name just a few.1 All these languages, however, mark their subjects invariably with the nominative case. Ergative languages have posed challenges to the AH in that many of them exhibit syntactic ergativity, a feature in which the absolutive arguments (intransitive subject and transitive object) relativize with a gap, but the ergative DP does not (Keenan and Comrie, 1977, 1979; Dixon, 1994; Aldridge, 2008). With the advent of processing studies, ergativity, with its dissociation between morphological case marking and grammatical function, offers a particularly promising area for the study of relativization, as it opens up a special dimension for a study of the interaction between syntax, morphology, and processing. In addition to conceptual considerations, it is worth noting that the processing of ergative languages has yet to be explored by the linguistic community, and the current study is an initial step in that direction. We present and analyze the results of an experiment that tests the processing of relative clauses in a head-final ergative language, Avar. The paper is organized as follows: Section 2 explains the logic of the study presented here. Section 3 is a brief overview of Avar, and section 4 presents the results of a behavioral experiment on Avar relativization. Section 5 provides a discussion of these results. Authors Affiliation * 1 University of Nijmegen, Nijmegen, The Netherlands. pim.mak@let.uu.nl * PMID: 18323073 * DOI: 10.3758/mc.36.1.170 Abstract Studies in several languages have shown that subject-relative clauses are easier to process than object-relative clauses. Mak, Vonk, and Schriefers (2006) have proposed the topichood hypothesis to account for the preference for subject-relative clauses. This hypothesis claims that the entity in the relative clause that is most topicworthy will be chosen as the subject. By default, the antecedent of the relative clause will be chosen as the subject of the relative clause, because it is the topic of the relative clause. However, when the noun phrase (NP) in the relative clause is also topicworthy, the preference for the antecedent to be the subject will disappear. This was confirmed in two experiments. In Experiment 1, we tested relative clauses with a personal pronoun in the relative clause. We obtained a preference for object-relative clauses, in line with the assumption that personal pronouns refer to a discourse topic and are thus topicworthy. In Experiment 2, the discourse status of the NP in the relative clause was manipulated; either it was not present in the preceding context, or it was the discourse topic. The experiment showed that when the NP in the relative clause refers to the discourse topic, the difficulty of object-relative clauses is reduced, in comparison with relative clauses with an NP that is new in the discourse, even in the absence of any explicit cue in the relative clause itself. The literature on subject preference in ergative relative clauses is strongest in Avar, Georgian, and related ergative-absolutive languages, with Avar being the earliest experimental focus and Georgian a later split-ergative test case. The Avar paper reports the first processing experiment on relativization in an ergative language with prenominal relatives, and it found no processing difference between the ergative subject gap and the absolutive object gap, while the absolutive subject gap was processed much faster [N3-F3]. Georgian work then extends this line by examining whether the generalization of subject preference holds in another ergative-absolutive language and reports ERP and self-paced reading evidence showing a large anterior negativity and slower reading times for object relative disambiguation compared with subject relative disambiguation [N1-F1]. In addition, the broader ergativity literature is contextualized by Polinsky et al. (2012) and Longenbaugh and Polinsky (2016; 2017) on Avar and Niuean, which are relevant because they are ergative or split-ergative languages and show that subject preference effects may not generalize across all ergative paradigms [N1-R2]. This makes Avar, Georgian, and Niuean the most studied ergative paradigms in the literature.

On whether subject preference is consistently observed, the evidence is mixed rather than uniform. In Avar, the study reports a strong absolutive-subject preference but no significant difference between ergative-subject and absolutive-object gaps, suggesting that morphological cueing and subject preference can cancel each other [N3-F3]. In Georgian, the evidence is more consistent with a subject preference advantage: ERP and reading-time results show slower processing for object relative disambiguation than for subject relative disambiguation [N1-F1]. The broader comparative literature on subject preference in other languages also indicates variability: the literature review in Lau (2021) notes that subject-gap processing advantage has been clearly observed in English, Dutch, German, French, Hebrew, Turkish, and Russian, but that Chinese and Cantonese show mixed results, with some studies favoring object relative clauses and others favoring subject relative clauses [N1-F1]. In Basque, recent work questions whether the generalization holds, and the review notes that the classic descriptive generalization may not extend to all ergative languages [N1-F1]. So the overall pattern is that subject preference is often observed, but it varies across languages and may be weaker or absent in some ergative contexts.

Preference is measured primarily through psycholinguistic tasks such as self-paced reading, ERP, and eye-tracking, with ERP and self-paced reading being especially prominent in the studies cited here. The Georgian study uses ERP and self-paced reading to show slower reading times and a large anterior negativity for object relative disambiguation compared with subject relative disambiguation [N1-F1]. The Avar study uses a behavioral experiment and reports reading-time results [N3-F3]. The broader literature review also cites a wide range of psycholinguistic measures, including self-paced reading, ERP, PET, fMRI, and eye-tracking, and emphasizes that these measures have consistently shown a subject processing advantage in English and several other languages [N1-F1]. The confound reported most explicitly is the interaction between linear distance and grammatical function: the literature review argues that relative clause processing profiles are driven by both the desire to interpret the gap as rapidly as possible (linear distance) and a desire to link gaps to subjects (subject preference), and that these factors can interact differently depending on language-specific properties [N1-F1]. The discourse-structure study further shows that discourse factors can modulate relative clause processing, with personal pronouns and discourse-topic NPs affecting preference and difficulty [N5-F4]. These confounds suggest that preference effects must be interpreted cautiously when grammatical structure, discourse context, and linear order covary.
node_outputs.N8: The literature on morphological and grammatical factors in relative clause processing emphasizes several features as particularly relevant: case marking, linear order, morphological cueing, and grammatical function. Case marking is especially important in ergative-absolutive systems because it dissociates grammatical function from morphological form; the Avar study notes that the ergative DP in a relative clause serves as a strong cue that favors the absolutive object gap [N3-F3]. The literature review also highlights that most of the languages studied are nominative-accusative, while Mandarin and Cantonese do not have overt morphological case, making them an important contrast case [N1-F1]. Linear order is another key factor: the literature review argues that in prenominal-relative languages, object relative clauses should be easier if processing depends mainly on filler-gap distance, but that this has not been consistently borne out, especially in Japanese and Korean, where subject relative clauses remain preferred despite shorter gap positions [N1-F1]. Morphological cueing is also central to the theoretical account in Avar, where the ergative DP cue helps project the remainder of the clause and reduces processing difficulty for the absolutive object gap [N3-F3]. Grammatical structure affects processing difficulty and ambiguity in several ways: the literature review states that subject-gap processing advantage has been clearly observed across many languages, but that Chinese and Cantonese show mixed results, indicating that grammatical structure can modulate processing profiles [N1-F1]. The discourse-structure study adds that discourse factors can guide sentence-level processing, with discourse-topic NPs reducing the difficulty of object relative clauses [N5-F4]. The relative clause attachment preferences literature also emphasizes that structural economy and pragmatic constraints can influence parsing decisions, with one study suggesting that parsing preferences may be shaped by richer functional domains or pragmatic cues [N4-R4]. Overall, the evidence suggests that morphology and syntax interact in relative clause interpretation by cueing the parser, determining linear order effects, and modulating the ease with which grammatical relations are assigned to the gap.

The studies that directly compare preference and morphology/grammar effects are best represented by the Avar and Georgian work. In Avar, the study explicitly combines subject preference with morphological cueing: it argues that subject preference would make ergative-subject and absolutive-subject gaps easier than absolutive-object gaps, but that the ergative DP in a relative clause serves as a strong cue favoring the absolutive object gap, so the two effects cancel out [N3-F3]. In Georgian, the study directly compares subject and object relative disambiguation using ERP and self-paced reading, showing slower processing for object relative disambiguation than for subject relative disambiguation, which is interpreted as evidence that subject preference persists in an ergative-absolutive language [N1-F1]. The broader literature review also frames the comparison in terms of linear distance versus grammatical function, noting that filler-gap distance accounts have been challenged by prenominal-relative data in Japanese and Korean, where subject preferences remain strong despite shorter gap positions [N1-F1]. The relative clause attachment preferences literature similarly addresses how parsing preferences are shaped by both structural and pragmatic factors, with studies suggesting that structural economy claims need to be evaluated against parsing preferences and that pragmatic constraints can modulate attachment choices [N4-R4]. 

Researchers control for preference versus grammatical complexity by manipulating relative clause position, gap location, and grammatical function. In Avar, the control comes from the comparison between ergative-subject, absolutive-subject, and absolutive-object gaps, allowing the authors to isolate the effects of subject preference from morphological cueing [N3-F3]. In Georgian, the control is provided by disambiguation tasks that force participants to resolve object versus subject relative clauses, enabling a direct comparison of processing difficulty across gaps [N1-F1]. The literature review also uses cross-linguistic comparisons across postnominal, prenominal, and split-ergative systems to control for linear order effects [N1-F1]. The discourse-structure study controls for discourse topic by varying whether the NP in the relative clause is present in the preceding context or is the discourse topic, showing that discourse factors can shift relative clause preferences [N5-F4]. The attachment preferences literature uses pragmatic constraints and parsing principles to control for factors other than grammatical structure [N4-R4]. The main interactions or trade-offs reported are cancellation between subject preference and morphological cueing in Avar, persistence of subject preference despite linear-order differences in Japanese and Korean, and modulation of parsing preferences by discourse topic, pragmatic constraints, and structural economy [N3-F3][N1-F1][N5-F4][N4-R4]. Overall, these studies show that preference and structure effects can reinforce, compete, or interact depending on the language and the experimental design.

The main theoretical accounts in the literature are centered on two broad claims: (1) that relative clause processing advantage comes from the desire to interpret the gap quickly, often linked to linear/temporal distance between the filler and the gap, and (2) that relativization on subjects is inherently easier to process because of grammatical-function preferences [N1-F1]. These claims are explicitly contrasted in the literature review, which argues that filler-gap distance and grammatical function are competing explanations for the subject-gap advantage [N1-F1]. The Avar study adds a third theoretical dimension: morphological cueing, where the ergative DP in a relative clause provides a cue that helps project the remainder of the clause and favors the absolutive object gap [N3-F3]. This makes morphological cueing a third mechanism that can interact with subject preference and grammatical function. The discourse-structure study further suggests that parsing is guided by discourse-topic status, so preference can be modulated by discourse context rather than only by grammatical structure [N5-F4]. The attachment preferences literature extends this by suggesting that parsing preferences may be shaped by structural economy, pragmatic constraints, and richer functional domains [N4-R4].

The most important methodological limitations are confounded variability across languages, confounded linear order, and confounded discourse context. The literature review notes that Chinese and Cantonese show mixed results, making it difficult to attribute differences solely to linear distance or grammatical function [N1-F1]. The same review reports that in Japanese and Korean, filler-gap distance effects have not fully accounted for the preference for subject relative clauses, implying that other factors must also be at work [N1-F1]. The discourse-structure study shows that discourse-topic NPs can reduce the difficulty of object relative clauses, so discourse factors are a confound that can shift preference [N5-F4]. The attachment preferences literature likewise warns that confounding factors such as pragmatic constraints and structural economy can distort parsing preferences [N4-R4]. Open empirical questions remain about how subject preference varies across ergative systems, whether the classic generalization holds universally, and whether the interaction between case marking, cueing, and grammatical function is fully captured by current measures [N1-F1][N3-F3]. The broader syntax-processing frameworks discussed in the evidence include filler-gap theories, accessibility hierarchies, structural economy, and pragmatic constraint models, but the literature suggests that these frameworks need to be integrated rather than treated as mutually exclusive [N1-F1][N3-F3][N4-R4]. Overall, the literature is still unresolved because preference and structure effects interact, and no single account explains all cross-linguistic variation consistently [N1-F1][N3-F3][N5-F4].

## Integrated synthesis: How existing studies describe the interaction between subject preference and morphological/grammatical factors in ergative relative clauses

The existing literature on ergative relative clauses is best understood as a conversation among three main themes: **subject preference**, **morphological/grammatical structure**, and **their interaction**. Across the branch reports, the evidence consistently shows that subject preference is not a universal or simple effect; rather, it varies across languages and can be strengthened, weakened, or even canceled out by grammatical and morphological factors. In ergative systems, case marking, linear order, cueing, and grammatical function all shape how relative clauses are processed, and these factors do not operate independently of one another.

### 1) Which ergative languages and paradigms are most studied?

The literature is strongest in **Avar**, **Georgian**, and other **ergative-absolutive** or **split-ergative** languages. Avar is especially central as the first experimental study of relativization in an ergative language with prenominal relatives [N3-F3]. Georgian then becomes an important later test case for whether the classic subject-preference generalization extends to another ergative-absolutive language [N1-F1]. Additional relevant paradigms include **Niuean** and other split-ergative systems, which are cited in the broader review literature as important contexts for comparing preference effects [N1-R2]. This makes Avar, Georgian, and related ergative-absolutive languages the most heavily studied ergative paradigms in the literature.

### 2) Whether subject preference is consistently observed or varies

The evidence is **mixed rather than uniform**. In **Avar**, the study reports no significant difference between the **ergative subject gap** and the **absolutive object gap**, while the **absolutive subject gap** is processed much faster [N3-F3]. That is, subject preference is still present, but it is not always the strongest or only effect at work. In **Georgian**, by contrast, the evidence is more consistent with a **subject preference advantage**: ERP and self-paced reading results show slower processing for object relative disambiguation than for subject relative disambiguation [N1-F1]. The broader comparative literature reinforces that subject-gap processing advantage is often observed across many languages, but it is not universal: **Chinese and Cantonese** show mixed results, and **Basque** has been cited as a language where the generalization may not hold [N1-F1].

So the overall pattern is that **subject preference is often observed**, but it varies across languages and can be **weakened or absent** in some ergative contexts. The literature therefore supports a **modular rather than deterministic** view of preference: it is a robust tendency, but not a universal rule.

### 3) How preference is measured and what confounds are reported

Preference is measured primarily through **psycholinguistic tasks** such as **self-paced reading**, **ERP**, and **eye-tracking**. The branch reports explicitly cite these as the main methods used in the literature [N1-F1][N3-F3]. In Avar, the study uses a behavioral experiment and reports reading-time results [N3-F3]. In Georgian, the study uses **ERP and self-paced reading** to compare object and subject relative disambiguation [N1-F1]. The literature review also notes that a wide range of psycholinguistic measures have been used to establish the subject-processing advantage in English and several other languages [N1-F1].

The main confounds reported in the literature are:

- **Linear distance vs. grammatical function**: the literature argues that relative clause processing profiles are driven by both the desire to interpret the gap as rapidly as possible (linear distance) and a desire to link gaps to subjects (subject preference), and that these factors can interact differently depending on language-specific properties [N1-F1].
- **Discourse context**: the discourse-structure study shows that discourse-topic NPs can reduce the difficulty of object relative clauses, indicating that parsing can be modulated by discourse factors [N5-F4].
- **Cueing and structure**: in Avar, the **ergative DP** serves as a strong cue that favors the **absolutive object gap**, creating a direct interaction between morphological cueing and subject preference [N3-F3].

These confounds are important because they show that preference effects cannot be interpreted in isolation: **linear order**, **case marking**, **cueing**, and **discourse context** all covary and can shift the observed preference pattern.

### 4) What morphological and grammatical factors are most relevant to relative clause processing

The literature emphasizes several key features as particularly relevant:

- **Case marking**: especially important in **ergative-absolutive systems**, where grammatical function is dissociated from morphological form. In Avar, the ergative DP in a relative clause serves as a strong cue that favors the absolutive object gap [N3-F3]. The literature review also notes that most of the languages studied are nominative-accusative, while Mandarin and Cantonese do not have overt morphological case, making them an important contrast [N1-F1].

The broader conclusion is that ergative relative clause processing is best understood as a dynamic interplay between **case marking**, **linear order**, **morphological cueing**, **grammatical function**, and **discourse context**, rather than as a simple preference for subject gaps alone.
